Songwriter Sharon Sheeley and singer Gene Vincent survived the crash, Cochran's current hit at the time was 'Three Steps to Heaven'. 1994: Pink Floyd started a four-week run at No.1 on the UK album chart with The Division Bell, their fourth No.1 album.

2004: Kurt Cobain's Mark IV-style Mosrite Gospel guitar sold for $117,500 at the Icons of 20th Century Music auction held in Dallas, Texas. Thank you. I know you agree on the importance of knowing the era and artists that shaped music for most people here. I can see it in the submissions on your friday night goatfest. As I've oft said "nothing truly dies until the last person talks about it". Maybe just a little raging against the dying of the light.

It really helps to understand the totality of the music if you know about the artist, the era, and the general public's perception of the artist. There are some songs which seem to play more passionately when I'm understanding more than just the rote and recreating the notes on the page. I'm not sure I have words to describe it, but there's a difference when (with certain songs) I know more of the story than just what's written in the music. I don't know if it results in a change that can be perceived, but it certainly can feel different.

I think it's the dualism of a piece of music. The emotion expressed and empathized through the technical production. As an example, take the early blues. Most of the artists wouldn't be considered (even by their own admission) as fluent or accomplished musicians. The playing was just a base to express what was felt. You can still feel their pain, frustration, passion in those recordings. I remember a video of BB King playing with U2 where he said "Y'all will need to play the chords, 'cause I don't play those". But as you move up the scale the evolution in technology (both instruments and recording capabilities) involved using that ability to enhance the expression. But for a good amount of time the emotion still ruled. Move along the scale and some artists, and profit-driven companies, started relying on the "wow" factor of flash to be the center. The emotional part became less and less a selling point, corporate focus groups decided what emotion was hot, and concocted what emotion sells and profits needed to be made. Thus we have todays major label crap being pushed. I'm thankful the internet has come as widespread as it has, allowing artists to get back to producing their own music apart from control of those who would limit what is heard. Maybe slowly some vestiges of emotional based expression will survive, aided but not controlled by technology.
